title: Cryogenic Recharacterization of a Commercial 22 nm FD-SOI Foundry Standard-Cell Library
authors: Mohamed Gharib, Rami Rasheedi, Salma Abdelzaher, Henry Shi, Mike Hammer, Llorenç Fanals-i-Batllori, Aldo Pena Perez, Antonino Miceli, Inna Partin-Vaisband
abstract: Wiring and bandwidth bottlenecks between a quantum processor and room-temperature electronics can be reduced by placing digital control at the cryogenic stage, but commercial foundry standard-cell libraries are not specified for operation at 4 K. A cryogenic recharacterization flow is therefore developed for a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI foundry standard-cell library using commercially available cryogenic compact-device models, while retaining the original cell circuits, layouts, logic functions, and implementation semantics and remaining compatible with the commercial synthesis, place-and-route, and signoff methodology used at room temperature. Body-bias dependence is quantified over 38,640 matched slew/load points at zero, +/-0.9 V, and +/-1.8 V body bias. Relative to full bias, zero-bias operation increases the median rising and falling delays by 38.6x and 33.0x, while approximately 90% of transitions exceed the foundry-defined maximum-transition envelope. The 0.8 V-to-0.4 V level shifter is even more sensitive to body bias: its worst-case falling delay decreases from 30.6 ns at zero bias to 0.56 ns at +/-1.8 V. For the outbound 0.4 V-to-0.8 V crossing, driving the 0.8 V receiver without a level shifter dissipates 57.7 uW of static power per bit at full bias, against 0.196 nW when level-shifted. In post-route analysis of the unchanged extracted physical database of a fabricated 32-bit ALU, the register-to-register setup boundary increases from 1.3 MHz at zero bias to 37.9 MHz at +/-0.9 V and 132.9 MHz at +/-1.8 V.
summary: This paper develops and applies a cryogenic recharacterization flow to a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI standard-cell library to enable digital control logic operation at 4 K. The research quantifies significant performance degradation and power changes compared to room temperature, highlighting the critical need for specialized cryogenic design methodologies for quantum computing control systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the bottleneck of interfacing quantum processors, which operate at cryogenic temperatures, with room-temperature classical control electronics.
main_result: The study quantifies the severe performance degradation (e.g., delay increases by factors of 33-38) and power issues when using standard commercial foundry libraries at 4 K, demonstrating the necessity of a cryogenic recharacterization flow.
method: A cryogenic recharacterization flow was developed for a 22 nm FD-SOI standard-cell library, involving extensive body-bias sweeping and post-route analysis of fabricated circuits.
model_or_system: The physical system is a commercial 22 nm FD-SOI foundry standard-cell library used to build digital control logic (like a 32-bit ALU) for quantum processors. The analysis models the behavior of these digital circuits at 4 K under various body biases.
key_observables: Median rising/falling delays, static power dissipation ($\mu	ext{W}/	ext{bit}$), setup boundary frequency (MHz), and transition violations.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperature (4 K), low core supply voltage (0.4 V), and forward body bias ($\pm 0.9 	ext{ V}, \pm 1.8 	ext{ V}$).
main_assumptions: The methodology assumes that recharacterizing the standard-cell library while retaining original layouts and semantics is sufficient for cryogenic compatibility.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the characterization flow, the physical layout of the ALU, and the dependence of cell timing and transition compliance on forward body bias.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of the cryogenic recharacterization flow, quantifies timing and power changes across various body biases, and validates the results using post-route analysis on a fabricated ALU test chip.
why_interesting: While the core focus is on semiconductor device physics and VLSI design, the direct application is enabling the classical control infrastructure necessary for scaling up quantum computing hardware.

The outlined 32-bit ALU occupies 399.97 × 58.96 µm of the 1000 × 1000 µm die; the remainder holds superconducting test structures outside the scope of this work [16].

Fig. 1. Characterization and implementation flow. The 1,326 timing-eligible cells are recharacterized at 4 K and 0.4 V, with body-bias dependence evaluated across three bias conditions. No cryogenic cell redesign is performed and foundry semantics are retained.

Fig. 3. Cell timing dependence on forward body bias at 4 K and 0.4 V, evaluated over 38,640 matched slew/load points. (a) Delay normalized to the ±1.8 V condition; markers denote medians and bars indicate the 10th–90th percentile range. (b) Fraction of 201,376 characterized output transitions exceeding the 0.7179 ns per-pin max_transition limit declared by the vendor library.

Fig. 4. The voltage-domain translator at 4 K. (a) Worst-case delay of the 0.8 V →0.4 V translator against forward body bias, for the smallest (V1_1) and largest (V1_16) drive. (b) Static current of the modeled outbound 0.4 V →0.8 V crossing, translator bypassed and in place. Bypassing under-drives the 0.8 V receiver and draws 72.2 µA per modeled path at ±1.8 V, against sub-nanoampere when translated.

Fig. 5. Seven-stage ring oscillator formed from the extracted commercial foundry INV_1 cell at fanout one. (a) Oscillation frequency versus supply; each curve ends at the lowest tested supply sustaining oscillation. (b) Energy– delay product (EDP), minima starred. Forward body bias reduces the minimum EDP by 1.52× at 4 K and 1.60× at 77 K against the 25 °C minimum. Dotted lines mark the ALU’s 0.4 V cryogenic and 0.65 V room-temperature supplies. Core-supply power is used; the simulated body-bias contribution stays below 3 × 10−3 % of ring power. The cryogenic Liberty is delivered at 0.4 V only; every other supply shown is a direct compact-model evaluation.
